entries.narration: Let's begin with three words that people use as if they meant one thing. Data is simply recorded facts: Asha, Bengaluru. A database is data that has been organised so that it can be found and trusted; the one we will use throughout this course is called shop. A database management system, a DBMS, is the software that stores that data, protects it, and answers questions about it. PostgreSQL is a DBMS. Now look at the board, and imagine Asha moves house. On the left, billing, shipping and reports each keep their own file, so there are three copies of Asha. Billing is updated, but the other two files still say Bengaluru. The business now has two truths, and nobody knows which one is right. On the right, the same three applications ask one DBMS. There is one copy, so there is one update, and every application sees it at once. The DBMS also enforces rules about what may be stored, controls who can see or change what, and lets many people work safely at the same time. A common misconception is that a database is just a spreadsheet with more rows. A spreadsheet stores values. A DBMS also enforces rules and coordinates writers. So the lesson is that copies drift apart, and a single governed copy cannot, and that SQL is the language we use to talk to the DBMS.

A relational database stores everything in tables, and the tables refer to one another. Let's name the parts using the two real tables on the board. A column is one attribute, such as city, and every value in it has the same type. A row is one record: one customer, or one order. A cell is where a row meets a column, and it holds one value, or no value at all. And a schema is a named folder of tables; ours is called shop, so the customers table is written shop dot customers. Now the idea that makes it relational. Look at the orders table: it has a customer I D column, and that number is the identifier of a row in the customers table. That link is a relationship. Asha is customer one, and she appears on orders one and three, so one customer can have many orders. Orders and products are related many-to-many, because an order has many products and a product appears on many orders, and a third table, order items, sits between them to record each pairing. Notice also Elena's phone cell, which says null. That means unknown, which is different from blank. A common misconception is that rows are kept in some order and columns are found by position. In fact, rows are a set, with no built-in order, and you find a column by its name. So a relationship is simply a column that holds another row's identifier.

A table on its own is just a list. Keys are what turn a set of tables into a database. A primary key identifies exactly one row, and it can never be null. In the orders table that is order I D. A key can also span several columns: an order line is identified by its order and its position within the order, so order items uses the pair, order I D and line number. A foreign key is a column that holds another table's key. Orders has a customer I D column, and every value in it must be the key of a real customer. Integrity means the database refuses rows that break these promises, and the three cards on the board show it happening. We try to create an order for customer ninety-nine, who does not exist, and the foreign key refuses. We try to delete customer one, but orders one, three and nine still point at them, so that is refused too. And we try to add order line one-one a second time, which breaks the primary key. The statements themselves are explained in chapters three and eight; for now, read the errors, because they name exactly which rule was broken. A common misconception is that the application will check these things. But then every program, every script and every person would have to check, and the database is the one place that sees all writers. So remember: a primary key promises uniqueness, and a foreign key promises existence.

Every column in a table has one type, and the type is a promise about every value that column will ever hold. The table at the top of the board shows five everyday types, each taken from a real column in our shop: integer for whole numbers, numeric for exact decimals such as prices, text for strings, date for calendar days, and boolean for true or false. If you try to put the word abc into an integer column, the database refuses it. Now the idea that trips up almost everyone: null. Null does not mean zero and it does not mean blank. It means the value is unknown or missing. Elena has no phone number on file, so her phone cell is null. Look at the three cards. Asking where phone is null finds Elena. Asking where phone equals null returns nothing at all, and raises no error, because comparing anything with null gives unknown, not true, and where only keeps rows that are true. And counting shows the same effect: there are nine customers, but count of phone says eight, because aggregate functions skip nulls. A common misconception is that null equals null is true. It is not; it is itself null. So always use is null, and its opposite, is not null. This is only the first look. Chapter four returns to null with the full three-valued logic.

A SQL statement is built from a small number of parts, and knowing them makes every statement readable. Keywords, such as select and from, are not case sensitive. Identifiers are the names of things, tables and columns, and when they are not quoted, PostgreSQL folds them to lower case, so upper-case first name works perfectly well. A quoted identifier, in double quotes, keeps its case exactly and must match it. Literals are values written into the statement: text in single quotes, numbers as they are, and a quote inside text is written by doubling it. Comments are ignored: two dashes to the end of the line, or slash star to star slash for a block. And a semicolon ends the statement. The most common beginner mistake is on the board. Double quotes do not make strings; they make identifiers. So select double-quote Asha asks for a column called Asha, and fails with: column Asha does not exist. Strings use single quotes. Finally, statements fall into five families by what they act on. D D L defines structure, D M L changes rows, D Q L asks questions with select, T C L groups changes into transactions, and D C L controls access. The card on the board runs one of each. Some books file select under D M L, but we keep it separate because it changes nothing.

SQL is a conversation, and it helps to be clear about who is speaking. The client, which might be psql, an application, or a notebook, sends the text of a statement. The server, here PostgreSQL, parses that text, plans how to answer it, executes the plan, and sends back rows together with a command tag. The server does the work; the client only shows the result. That answers a common misconception: your computer did not run the query, the server did. Next, dialects. SQL is a standard, but each product speaks its own version of it. On the board, the same request, give me three customers, is written two ways. Limit three is PostgreSQL's spelling, and fetch first three rows only is the standard one, and PostgreSQL accepts both. Other products may accept only one of them, and the way to find out is to read that product's documentation. Notice that order by decides which three rows come back; without it, no particular three are promised. Finally, an annotated tour of the shop. This one query counts the rows in each of the four core tables: nine customers, ten products, eleven orders and sixteen order lines. Four more tables, categories, employees, payments and reviews, join the story as we need them. If you want to follow along, you can run these queries yourself, but that is entirely optional. We can now describe relational data. Next, we translate business requirements into structures and enforceable rules.

A database design starts as sentences about the business, so the first skill is reading them carefully. Nouns, such as customer, order and product, become entities, and each entity becomes a table. Verbs, such as places or contains, describe relationships between entities. For every relationship, ask how many are on each side. That is its cardinality. The table on the board turns six real sentences about our shop into structure. A customer places many orders: that is one-to-many, and it becomes a foreign key on the many side, the customer I D column in orders. An online order has no sales rep: that is an optional relationship, so the employee I D column is allowed to be null. Now the sentence that surprises beginners: an order has many products, and a product appears on many orders. That is many-to-many, and a relationship like that cannot be stored in a single column on either side. It needs a table of its own. In the drawing, orders one and three are paired with four real products through the order items table, one row per pairing. And a fact about the pairing, such as the price actually paid, belongs on that table, not on the product. A common misconception is that one table per noun is enough. The relationships need homes too. And remember the limitation: a schema is only as right as the sentences it was built from.

Normalisation is the discipline of storing each fact once, in the table about whatever determines that fact. The key idea is a dependency: the value of one column is fixed by another. A customer's city depends on the customer, not on any particular order. The wide sheet at the top ignores that. It repeats Asha's name and city on every one of her orders. Now watch what happens when she moves. The card in the middle builds that sheet from the real orders and customers tables, updates only one of her three rows, and counts. Bengaluru appears on two rows, Mysuru on one. The database now holds two truths about one person, and nothing in it says which is right. That is an update anomaly. There are two more. An insert anomaly: you cannot record a customer who has not ordered yet, because there is no row to put them in. And a delete anomaly: removing a customer's last order could remove every trace of them. The cure is on the bottom. Split the sheet by who each fact is about. The city lives on one customer row, orders refer to the customer, and an update changes one place. The formal names are first normal form, one value per cell; second, depending on the whole key; and third, depending on the key and nothing but the key. A common misconception is that more tables is always better. Normalise for correctness, and relax it later only for a measured need. This is an introduction; formal dependency theory is out of scope.

Every table lives inside something, and two levels of containment do the organising. A PostgreSQL server can run many databases, and when you connect, you connect to exactly one of them. Inside a database there are schemas, and a schema is a named folder that holds tables. The drawing shows our shop schema with its tables, and a second schema, staging, that has its own table also called customers. Two tables with the same name can coexist because they live in different schemas. Creating a database uses create database, which cannot run inside a transaction. Creating a schema is just create schema, and that can be rolled back. Now the practical question: when you write select from customers, which one do you get? An unqualified name is looked up along the search path, in order, and the first schema with a match wins. On the right, we put staging first, and the count comes back zero, because the empty staging table shadows the real one. That is the kind of surprise to avoid, so qualify names in any script you share. A common misconception is that a schema is a separate database. One query can use many schemas, but it cannot reach into another database: PostgreSQL says cross-database references are not implemented. So schemas separate names, while databases separate everything.

A table definition is a name followed by a list of columns, and each column is a name and a type. The type is a promise about every value in the column, so choose the narrowest type that is always true. Numeric with two numbers, precision and scale, is an exact decimal: numeric eight comma two holds eight digits in all, two of them after the point. A default fills in a column you leave out of an insert, and a column with no default becomes null. And an identity column lets the database number the rows for you. The dictionary at the top describes a wishlist table, which records which customer wants which product, a small extension to our shop. The first card creates it and inserts a row naming only two columns. The result shows six values stored: priority and the gift flag from their defaults, and the note as null. The second card shows precision at work. Twelve point three four five stored in numeric eight two is rounded to twelve thirty-five. A number too large for the declared precision is refused with numeric field overflow. And the comparison explains why money must not be a floating point number: zero point one plus zero point two equals zero point three is true for numeric and false for floating point, because floats are binary approximations. The last card shows an identity column assigning ids one and two. The full catalogue of types is out of scope here.

A key is a promise about uniqueness, and the database refuses to let you break it. A primary key identifies exactly one row. It is unique, it can never be null, and a table can have only one. Our wishlist uses a composite primary key, made of customer I D and product I D together, which means a customer may wish for a given product only once. In the first card we insert the pair one and four, then insert it again. The second insert fails with a duplicate key error that names the constraint, wishlist underscore pkey. A unique constraint is similar, but a table may have many of them, and unlike a primary key it allows nulls, because unknown is not considered equal to unknown. The customers table has one on email, so inserting a second customer with an existing email is refused, and the error names customers email key. Both errors name the constraint, and those are the names we will read from the database's own metadata shortly. How do you choose a key? A surrogate key is a number with no meaning, such as customer I D. A natural key is data that identifies the row by itself, like our pair. Email is unique, but people change their email, which makes it a poor primary key. A common misconception is that unique and primary key are the same thing. One identifies the row; the other is a rule about a column.

Constraints keep bad records out, no matter who or what is writing them. There are three guards on the finished wishlist table. Not null says a column must have a value. A foreign key says the value must exist in the parent table: every customer I D on the wishlist must belong to a real customer. And a check constraint says the value must satisfy a rule, here that priority is between one and five. The table on the board is the exercise to follow with your own reasoning: six candidate records, and for each, will it be accepted? The first two, customer one with product four and customer three with product five, satisfy every rule, so they are accepted. The pair one-four a second time repeats the primary key. Customer ninety-nine has no parent row, so the foreign key refuses it. Priority nine fails the check. And a null customer fails not null. Each is refused by one named rule, and the error says which, so you can read the cause directly. Foreign keys also force a decision about the children. By default, deleting a parent that still has children is refused. With on delete cascade, deleting the parent deletes its children too, and the bottom card shows it: customer seven had two wishes, and after deleting her, none are left. A common misconception is that the application can enforce all this. But then every program, script and person would have to, and the database is the one place that sees every writer.

A database can describe itself, and it does so in tables that you can query like any other. The SQL standard defines a set of views for this called information schema. Behind them sits a catalogue, the system's own tables, and that part is specific to each product: in PostgreSQL it is called pg catalog. Another product's catalogue will differ, so read its documentation before relying on it. The three cards on the board ask three ordinary questions. First, which tables are there? The answer is eight tables, with between three and eight columns each. Second, which columns does the orders table have, and may they be null? Only employee I D may be null, which matches the business rule that online orders have no sales rep. Third, which keys does orders have? One primary key, and two foreign keys, and notice that their names are exactly the names that appeared in the error messages in the last two sections. That is why metadata matters: it lets you read an unfamiliar schema before writing a query against it, and check that a constraint you expect really exists. A common misconception is that metadata needs a separate tool. It is just data, and you query it with SQL. If you follow along, running these queries is optional, and the answers are on the board.

Structures change over time, and alter table is how you change them without losing the rows. The script on the left starts with the wishlist as we built it, then makes three changes. It adds an owner column that is not null with a default of one; it renames added on to added; and it changes the type of priority from integer to bigint. The two diagrams show the shape before and after, so you can compare them by eye: one new column, one new name, one new type, and every existing row is still there. Drop column is different, because the data in that column is gone for good. Now the trap that catches everyone once. If you add a not null column to a table that already has rows, PostgreSQL refuses, saying the column contains null values, because the existing rows would have nothing in it. There are two ways out: give the column a default, or add it as nullable, fill it in, and then set it not null. For safety, rehearse a structure change inside a transaction, because in PostgreSQL structure changes can be rolled back, and remember that on very large tables some changes lock or rewrite the whole table. A common misconception is that alter table only changes the definition. It can change every row.

Three statements remove things, and each removes something different. Delete, which we meet in chapter eight, removes the rows you choose and leaves the table. Truncate empties all the rows of a table, and does it fast, but the table itself stays: its columns, constraints and indexes are still there. In the first card we put two rows in, truncate, and count zero. Drop table goes further: it removes the table and its rows. In the second card, a select after the drop fails, saying the relation does not exist. Now the protection that dependencies give you. Trying to drop the customers table is refused, because orders and reviews depend on it through foreign keys, and the error detail lists exactly which ones. You could add cascade to drop those constraints as well, but read the detail first and be sure that is what you want. Adding if exists makes a drop safe to re-run. And here is the reassuring part: in PostgreSQL all three can be rolled back inside a transaction. I checked that a rolled-back truncate brings the rows back and a rolled-back drop brings back the table. Outside a transaction, though, they are final, so take a backup first. A common misconception is that truncate is just a faster delete. It skips the per-row work, and it is refused on tables that other tables reference. The schema now expresses the business rules but holds no useful records. Next, we populate and validate it.

Insert adds rows to a table, and every row is tested against the rules we defined in chapter two. The safest form names the columns you are supplying, followed by the values in the same order. Look at the first card. We supply four columns of the products table, and the other two take their defaults. The returning clause asks PostgreSQL to print the row as it was stored, and you can see stock is zero and discontinued is false, both filled in by defaults. The second card shows the positional form, with no column list. It works, but only if you supply all six values in exactly the table's column order, so it breaks the day someone adds a column. A common misconception is that the shorter form is the better one; in practice it is the more fragile. The third card adds three rows in one statement, by repeating the parenthesised list. PostgreSQL reports insert zero three, and the product count goes from ten to thirteen. A word on safety, because this is the first statement that changes data. Always look at the command tag. Insert zero three means three rows were added, and if you expected one, something is wrong. So the lesson is to name your columns, and to add many rows in one statement rather than many statements.

Letting the database fill in values is convenient, but it helps to understand exactly what it does. A default fills a column you leave out of an insert, and a column with no default becomes null. An identity column goes further, and comes in two flavours: generated always, where the database chooses and you may not, and generated by default, where you may supply a value. Look at the first card. We insert gift, then insert temp and undo that, then insert sale. The ids are one and three. The undone row still used up the number two, because sequences are deliberately not transactional, so gaps are normal and ids are never guaranteed to be consecutive. The second card shows that generated always refuses an explicit id. The third shows the trap with generated by default: we insert ninety-nine by hand, the sequence does not notice, and the next automatic id is one. It will reach ninety-nine one day and collide, so prefer generated always. The last card is about optional values. A value can be absent in four ways: left out, written as default, written as null, or written as an empty string. Only the first three are null. The empty string is a real value, which is why count of phone says nine, not eight. Two misconceptions fall away here: ids are not consecutive, and blank is not missing. Pick one way of saying no value, usually null, and stay with it.

Every row you insert must pass every rule, and the rules give loading a direction. When a row breaks a constraint, the statement stops with an error that names the rule that was broken. And a statement is all or nothing, so no row is ever half-stored. The first card shows it. We insert two products in one statement. The first is perfectly valid. The second has a negative price and breaks a check constraint. PostgreSQL rejects the whole statement, and the good row is not kept either. I confirmed that by checking the table afterwards, because a script stops at its first error and cannot show the aftermath itself. A common misconception is that an error leaves half the rows loaded. It leaves none. The second part is about order. Foreign keys mean a row cannot point at something that does not exist yet, so related tables must be loaded parents first. The chain on the board is the workable order for the shop: categories, products, customers, orders, order lines, and finally payments. The bottom card shows the same rule as an error. We try to add a line for order fourteen, which does not exist yet, and the foreign key refuses it. So when you see a constraint error, read the constraint name, and then decide whether the row is wrong or the order is.

Copy loads a whole file in one statement, and it is far faster than a series of inserts. Plain copy with a file name makes the server read the file, which needs special privileges. The psql command backslash copy reads a file from your own machine. And copy from standard in takes the data inline, ended by a line with backslash dot, which is what the cards on the board do, so they need no file. The safe pattern, drawn at the top, is to load into a staging table, validate the data, and only then insert it into the real table. The first card has a bad value, the word five where a number belongs. The whole load is rejected, and the error context names the line and the column, so you know what to fix. Nothing was loaded, because the load is atomic. The second card is the more interesting case. This load is clean: copy four, four rows loaded. But the validation queries reveal two problems. One row refers to customer ninety-nine, who does not exist, and the pair one-four appears twice. Those queries use joins and grouping that chapters four and five explain; for now, read the results. A common misconception is that copy checks your business rules. It checks types and the target table's constraints, nothing more. A load can succeed and still be wrong, which is why you validate before you trust it. Loader-specific options are out of scope here.

Here is the whole chapter in one worked case. A feed of six new customers arrives as a file. We load it into a staging table as plain text, so that nothing is refused on the way in, and then we give every row a verdict: loaded, or rejected with a reason. The long card on the left does exactly that, and the result is the comparison between the source file and the rows that will load. Rows ten, eleven and fifteen are fine and are loaded. Row twelve has no email, which the not null rule forbids. Row thirteen uses an email that already belongs to Asha, which the unique rule forbids. And row fourteen has a date that cannot exist, the fourteenth of month thirteen. Each rejection has a reason that traces back to a rule from chapter two. Then we reconcile. The source had six rows, three were loaded and three were rejected, so six equals three plus three, and the customers table grew from nine rows to twelve. I checked those counts by running the whole process. A common misconception is that no error means the load was correct. It does not. You have to compare what was loaded with what the source contained, and every row must be accounted for. The assumption here is that the feed's columns are complete; a real feed needs more checks. The database now contains validated records. Next, we turn those records into answers to business questions.

A select statement chooses columns, and its result is a new table. Three ideas matter here. An alias, introduced with as, gives an output column a new name; it changes the label, never the data. Distinct removes duplicate rows from the result. And the grain of a result is what one row of it means. Look at the board. Selecting the status of every order returns eleven rows, because the grain is one row per order. Selecting distinct status returns four rows, because the grain is now one row per kind of status. And distinct city gives eight rows for nine customers, because two of our customers live in Lyon. The result is shorter, but the customers table is unchanged. A common misconception is that distinct cleans the data. It does not remove anything from the table; it hides duplicates in one result. That matters because duplicates are sometimes a problem to fix and sometimes simply the truth. So before you read any result, ask what one row of it means. That habit prevents many wrong summaries, and we will use it again when we group and join. Queries here are written for PostgreSQL, and the columns we choose are only the ones we ask for.

The where clause is a filter. For every row, the database evaluates your condition and keeps the row only if the answer is true. You compare with equals, not equals, less than and greater than, with or without equals, and you combine conditions with and, or, and not. The first card shows an and: of the eleven orders, three are delivered and dated from the second of March, orders three, four and five. Now the trap on the second card. And binds more tightly than or, so the condition pending or shipped and customer two does not mean what it seems to say. It means pending, or else shipped by customer two. It returns four orders: six, nine, ten and eleven. Put parentheses around the or, so that the condition reads pending or shipped, and then customer two, and exactly one order qualifies, order six. A common misconception is that conditions are read left to right. Precedence decides, not position. Remember also that text goes in single quotes and that equality is a single equals sign. The rule to take away is simple: whenever you mix and with or, add parentheses to say exactly what you mean.

In, between and like are three shorthands for conditions you could write out longhand. In means equal to one of a list. The first card asks for customers in London, Lyon or Milan and finds four, with Lyon appearing twice because two customers live there. Between means within a range, and it is inclusive at both ends. The second card asks for prices between twenty-nine ninety and forty-four, and the result contains the book at exactly twenty-nine ninety and the other at exactly forty-four. A common misconception is that between excludes its ends; it includes them. Like matches patterns: percent stands for any text, and underscore for a single character. The third card shows that like is case sensitive in PostgreSQL. The pattern lowercase c percent finds two email addresses, while uppercase C percent finds none, and no error tells you so. You simply get an empty result. Pattern matching rules differ between products, so check the documentation of the one you use. The lesson is that each shorthand has a precise boundary, and reading that boundary carefully is what keeps a query honest.

Logic in SQL has three values: true, false, and unknown. A comparison with null is unknown, never true, and where keeps only rows that are true. The table at the top shows how and and or behave across the three values. And with false is always false, even when the other side is unknown, because no value could make it true. Or with true is always true. Anything else involving unknown stays unknown. The first card asks the server to confirm four of those cells, and it agrees. Now the consequence on real data, in the second card. We ask for customers whose phone is not equal to Asha's number. The answer is seven, not eight, because Elena's phone is null, the comparison is unknown, and her row is quietly dropped. Is distinct from treats null as an ordinary value, and returns eight. A common misconception is that not equal includes the nulls. It does not. So whenever a column can be null, ask yourself what unknown does to your where clause. Chapter one introduced is null; here is the full reason it exists.

Expressions compute a value for each row, and the types involved decide the answer. You can use plus, minus, times, divide and remainder on columns and literals. The first card adds eighteen percent to two real prices and rounds to two places, so money stays at two decimals: sixty-nine sixty-two and thirty-five twenty-eight. The second card is the classic trap. Seven divided by two is three, not three and a half, because dividing two whole numbers truncates. Make one side exact, as in seven divided by two point zero, and you get three point five. A common misconception is that dividing integers gives a fraction. The third card converts explicitly. Cast turns the text twelve into a number, and double colon turns a text into a date, so adding thirty days gives the thirty-first of March. The last card shows a conversion that cannot succeed. Turning abc into an integer is an error, not a guess, and that is a good thing: you find out immediately. The habit to build is to know the type on both sides of every operator. Conversion rules differ between products, so these are PostgreSQL's.

A function takes values and returns a value, row by row, and there are three families worth knowing first. Text functions include upper, length, left, and the double bar to join strings. In the first card, Asha's email has twenty characters, and by taking everything left of the at sign we extract the handle, asha dot rao, while the double bar builds the full name. Numeric functions include round, ceiling, floor and absolute value. Rounding twenty-nine ninety times one point one eight to one place gives thirty-five point three. Date functions are where care matters most. A date plus an integer is a date that many days later, so order one plus seven days is the eighth of March. Extract pulls out a part, such as the month. And subtracting one date from another gives a plain number of days: the twelfth minus the first is eleven. A common misconception is that function names are standard across products. Many are not, and date arithmetic especially varies. These are PostgreSQL's, so check the documentation for the product you use. And always know what type a function returns.

Case lets a query return a value that depends on a condition. You write when, then, optionally else, and end. The branches are tested in order, and the first true one wins. If nothing matches and there is no else, the result is null. The first card sorts five products into price tiers: budget under thirty, mid under a hundred, premium otherwise. Wireless earbuds and the desk lamp are mid, the headphones and laptop are premium, and the SQL book at twenty-nine ninety is budget. Now the second card, where the same branches are reordered. When under a hundred comes first, the SQL book matches it and is labelled mid. The budget branch can never be reached. A common misconception is that the branches are independent. They are not: the order is part of the meaning. So put the narrowest condition first and always include an else. The third card shows coalesce, a related tool that substitutes a fallback for a null. Elena has no phone, so she shows as no phone. Case is also how you build date and range buckets, and we will use it again when we summarise.

A table has no order, and a query result has none either, unless you ask for one with order by. Limit keeps the first rows, but of that order, so limit without order by returns an unspecified set of rows. The first card shows the other half of the story: ties. Orders one and two share a date, so ordering by date alone does not say which comes first, and the answer could change between runs. Adding the order identifier as a tie-breaker makes the order deterministic. The second card is about pagination, showing page two of size three in two ways. Offset skips three rows and takes three. Keyset pagination remembers the last key seen, here three, and continues after it. Both return orders four, five and six, but only because the order is total. Offset gets slower as you page deeper, and keyset needs a unique ordering key, trade-offs we revisit in chapter seven. The third card shows where nulls sort. PostgreSQL puts them last when ascending, so we ask for nulls first, and the orders with no sales rep come to the top. Other products differ, so check. A page is only stable if the order is total.

Aggregate functions turn many rows into one: count, sum, average, minimum and maximum. They skip nulls, as we saw in chapter one. The first card summarises the eight payments in a single row: a total of twenty-two forty-eight seventy, an average of two eighty-one oh nine, a smallest of seventy-three ninety and a largest of eight ninety-nine. Group by goes further and makes one bucket per value, so you get one summary row per group. Follow the lower board. The where clause runs first and drops the cancelled order. Group by customer then gathers the ten remaining orders into six buckets. Having now judges each bucket: only those whose count is above one survive, which are customers one, two and four. The contrast is on the second card. Putting count in a where clause is an error, because at that step the groups do not exist yet. A common misconception is that having is just where for groups. It runs later, on groups. So a condition on a column belongs in where, and a condition on an aggregate belongs in having. Reading the result correctly also depends on the grain: each row here is one customer.

A query is read in a different order from the order in which it is written, and that logical order defines the result. It runs from, then where, group by, having, select, distinct, order by, and finally limit. The engine is free to execute the query physically in another order, which chapter seven explores, as long as the result is the same as the logical order would give. That one picture explains many errors. In the first card, we filter on sale price, an alias created in select. Where is step two and select is step five, so the alias does not exist yet, and PostgreSQL says the column does not exist. The second card repeats the expression in where, which works, and order by may use the alias because it comes after select. The third card is an incorrect summary. A report says there are nine customers. As a count of rows, that is correct. As a count of people, it is wrong, because customers three and nine are the same person recorded twice, so there are eight. Nothing failed; the question was ambiguous. A common misconception is that the database runs the query as written. Before trusting any summary, check its grain. Single-table reports reveal only part of the business story. Next, we connect related records and query results.

Combining tables starts with a question: how many rows will come out? A join pairs rows, so the answer depends on the relationship between the tables. A foreign key links a many row to its one row. One customer has many orders, one order has many lines, and each line points to one product. The board shows the four tables with their row counts. Now read the three cards. Counting orders alone gives eleven: the grain is one order. Joining orders to their lines gives sixteen, because each order now appears once for every line it has, so the grain became one line. Joining orders to their customer gives eleven again, because each order has exactly one customer and nothing is repeated. This is the misconception to avoid: joining does not just add columns, it can multiply rows. The assumption is a foreign key that matches the direction you expect; the limitation is that the counts here describe this small dataset only. Before writing any join, state the grain you expect afterwards, and compare it with what comes back.

An inner join keeps a pair of rows only when the on condition is true. Think of trying each order against each customer and keeping the pairs that match. Aliases such as c and o say which table each column comes from, which keeps the query readable. The first card joins on the foreign key. It returns eleven pairs, one per order, and the four shown are the first by order number. Customers seven and eight never ordered, so no pair contains them: unmatched rows disappear. The second card is the failure to recognise. The condition compares the customer number with the order number. The query runs without any error and returns nine rows that look plausible, but order three belongs to Asha, and here it is paired with Chloe. The server cannot know what you meant. So join a foreign key to the key it references, and spot-check a few rows against what you expect. The limitation of the inner join is exactly what we saw: anything without a partner is lost, which is what the next section addresses.

An outer join solves the loss of unmatched rows. A left join keeps every row from the left table, and where nothing matches, it fills the right-hand columns with null. The first card shows customers seven and eight present, with blank orders. Testing the right key for is null after the join finds exactly the unmatched rows, as the second card shows: that pattern is called an anti-join. Now the important detail, predicate placement. The third card puts the status filter inside on, so the filter decides which rows match. All nine customers stay, giving ten rows, five of them matched. The fourth card puts the same filter in where, which runs after the join. The padded rows have a null status, so they are removed, leaving five rows. The outer join has been silently undone. These counts are real output from the server. So when a condition concerns the right table and you want to keep the left rows, put it in on, and use where only for conditions you truly want to remove rows.

Sometimes the two sides of a join are the same table. Employees have a manager id that points at another employee. To read it, we use the table twice under two aliases: e for the employee and m for the same table read as the manager. A left join keeps the chief executive, whose manager is null. Aliases are what make this readable. The opposite case is the cross join, which has no condition and returns every pairing. Nine customers with ten products give ninety rows. That can be useful on purpose, for example to build every combination, but it is a trap by accident. The second card joins employees to themselves on a condition that is always true, and returns forty-nine rows, seven times seven, with no error at all. The misconception is that a forgotten condition produces an error; it produces far too many rows. The assumption in a self-join is a key that points back into the same table, and the limitation is that a single self-join reads only one level of the hierarchy, a point we return to with recursion later.

Real questions need more than two tables, and each additional join can change the number of rows. Look at order one on the board. It has two lines and one payment. When we join orders to lines and to payments, the single payment of one hundred eighteen eighty is repeated on both line rows. That is duplicate amplification. Now summing over the whole shop: the payments table alone totals twenty-two forty-eight seventy, which is the true figure. Summing the payment amount after joining through the lines gives thirty-three twenty-one forty, because every payment is counted once per line. Nothing failed; the query simply answered a different question than the one we asked. The fix is to bring each side to the order grain before joining. Aggregate the payments per order, take the distinct orders that have lines, and then join. The total matches again. The habit to build is to check the grain after every join, and to sum only at the grain where the value lives.

A subquery is a query written inside another query. It comes in two shapes. A scalar subquery returns one row with one column, and you use it wherever a value fits. The first card compares each price with the average price, one hundred fifty point forty-four, and only the laptop is above it. A table subquery returns a set of rows. With in, it supplies a list: the second card finds the customers who have a pending order, which are one, four and nine. In the from clause, the same idea is called a derived table: the third card first counts orders per customer, then filters on that count, a way to use an aggregate as an ordinary column. The contrast is the last card. If something that must be a single value produces two rows, PostgreSQL reports an error, since the price in category six matches two products. Before writing a subquery, decide whether the inner query should produce one value or a set, and shape it accordingly.

A correlated subquery refers to a column of the outer row, so it cannot run on its own. Logically, for each outer row, the inner query is evaluated with that row's value. The first card keeps the products priced above the average of their own category. The trace table follows one row: for Studio Headphones in category six, the inner query computes the average price of category six, which is one hundred four, and since one forty-nine is greater, the row stays. The third card shows the averages for each category, so you can check every comparison by eye. Five of ten products pass. That is the logical order; the engine is free to plan it differently, as chapter seven will show. Correlated subqueries also work in the select list. The last card counts orders for each customer, and customers seven and eight receive a zero, whereas a join followed by grouping would have dropped them. The misconception is that the inner query runs once: logically it depends on the row, and that dependence is what makes it correlated.

Exists asks one question: is there at least one matching row? It returns true or false, so the columns inside the subquery do not matter, and it never duplicates the outer row. The last card finds customers with a pending order: one, four and nine. Now the pitfall. We want the employees who handled no order. Not exists answers correctly: five employees. Not in gives zero rows, with no error. Why? The orders table contains nulls in employee id, because online orders have no sales representative. A value tested against a list containing null cannot be proven absent. The third card shows it in miniature: one not in four, five is true, but one not in four, null is null, and where keeps only true. So the two operators are only equivalent when the list can never contain null. Use not exists for the question has no match, or filter the nulls out of the list explicitly. This is the null logic from chapter four, now causing a real query to return nothing.

Set operators combine whole result sets instead of joining rows side by side. Both queries must have the same number of columns and compatible types. By default, they remove duplicates; the all variants keep them. Our inputs are the customer numbers from eleven orders and from nine reviews. Union all simply stacks them: twenty rows. Union removes duplicates, leaving seven distinct customers, one to six and nine. Intersect keeps those in both: one to five, the customers who ordered and also reviewed. Except keeps those only in the first query: six and nine, who ordered but never reviewed. The all variants of intersect and except exist in PostgreSQL, though not in every database, and they count multiplicity: intersect all returns nine rows here. The last card shows the shape rule being enforced: a different number of columns is an error. The common misconception is that union only appends. It also sorts or hashes to remove duplicates, so use union all when duplicates are impossible or acceptable.

A view gives a query a name. The first card defines order totals as a join of orders with their lines, grouped per order, and then queries it like a table. Only the definition is stored, not the rows; each use runs the underlying query on the current data. So a view hides the join and the grouping behind a simple name, and a change to the base tables shows up in the next read; that behaviour is checked in a hidden test. The cost is not hidden, though, because the join still runs. Updates are the limitation. The second card creates a simple view over orders and updates a row through it; the base table changes. The third card tries to update a view that contains group by, and PostgreSQL refuses, because one view row stands for many base rows. Whether a view is updatable depends on its definition, and the rules vary between databases. A view is not a copy of the data but a saved query, and comparing it with the underlying query is the test of whether you understood it. We can connect the necessary evidence; next we express sequences, comparisons, and multi-step analytical questions.
